problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.

activity_context.topic_title: Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Euclidean Spaces (Orthogonal Bases)

feedback.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -16 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{(-18)\cdot (-2)+(-16)\cdot 2+1\cdot 4}{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}v=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{(-18)\cdot (-3)+(-16)\cdot 3+1\cdot (-3)}{(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}w=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
